opus-5.5.text:
I think the valuations are one of the more informative signals we have about what investors expect from AI, so it's worth reading them carefully.

If you look at a company like Nvidia, its market cap reflects not just current revenue but the discounted value of expected future cash flows. When you back out what that implies, you find investors are pricing in sustained, very large growth in spending on AI compute, well beyond what you'd get by extrapolating the old trends in data center or gaming demand. The same is true, to a lesser degree, for TSMC and ASML. They sit further up the supply chain, so their valuations also reflect expectations that leading-edge fab capacity and lithography equipment will be in high demand for years.

But I'd make two points about how to interpret this.

First, these valuations are large compared with historical semiconductor valuations, but small compared with what you'd expect if markets fully believed that AI could automate a large share of cognitive labor. Global labor compensation is something like fifty trillion dollars a year. If you thought AI systems could substitute for a meaningful fraction of that, the value of the hardware those systems run on would plausibly be far larger than what's currently priced in. So the market seems to expect AI to be a big deal, roughly on the scale of a major new technology platform, but not a transformative, growth-accelerating technology. In that sense the valuations are a kind of lower bound on the bullish view, not a confirmation of it.

Second, there's real headroom on the spending side. Total spending on AI training and inference hardware is still a small fraction of global GDP, even after the rapid growth of the last few years. Historically, when a technology offers large returns, investment can scale to percentage points of GDP. Think of railroads in the nineteenth century, or electrification. If AI keeps delivering capabilities people will pay for, there's no obvious economic reason compute spending couldn't grow by another order of magnitude or more. The binding constraints are more likely physical and industrial: fab capacity, advanced packaging, high-bandwidth memory, power and data center build-out. Those take years to expand, which is partly why the companies controlling the bottlenecks command such premiums.

So my overall read is that the valuations tell us sophisticated investors take AI scaling seriously, but they're still pricing in a fairly conservative scenario relative to what you'd expect if the more ambitious forecasts about AI's economic impact turn out to be right. If those forecasts start to look more credible, I'd expect both the valuations and the actual spending on compute to have a lot of room to grow.

r001.rationale: It says AI hardware spending remains a small fraction of GDP and that investment in technologies such as railroads and electrification has historically reached percentage points of GDP, showing room for compute spending to grow.

r002.rationale: It directly attributes chip-company valuations to investors pricing in sustained, substantial future growth in AI compute spending.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about this is that those valuations are, in a sense, the market making a bet about the future scale of compute spending. If you look at something like Nvidia, it's trading at a valuation that only makes sense if you expect the demand for AI accelerators to continue growing at a very rapid pace for many years. And that's consistent with what we've been seeing in the trends: training compute for frontier models has been growing by roughly four to five times per year, and the spending on hardware has been growing in tandem with that.

But I'd be a little careful here. There are a few different things going on. One is that the market is forward-looking, so some of this is already priced in, and the valuation reflects expectations rather than what's currently being spent. Another is that these companies occupy fairly unusual positions in the supply chain. TSMC and ASML, in particular, are close to monopolies in what they do. There's essentially one company that can produce leading-edge lithography machines, and effectively one company that can manufacture the most advanced chips at scale. So part of what you're seeing in the valuations is the market assigning value to that bottleneck position, not just to the raw growth of compute demand.

Now, if you ask how much more could be spent, I think the honest answer is that we're still quite far from any hard ceiling. Right now the largest training runs are costing on the order of hundreds of millions to a few billion dollars. Compare that to the revenues of the big tech companies, which are in the hundreds of billions per year, or to the scale of things like the Apollo program or the Manhattan Project as a fraction of GDP. If AI turns out to be as economically valuable as some people think, you could imagine spending that's one or two orders of magnitude larger than today before you start hitting the constraints of what the global economy could plausibly devote to this.

The more binding constraints, I think, are on the supply side rather than the willingness to spend. Fab capacity takes years to build. The capital expenditures for a leading-edge fab are tens of billions of dollars. Energy and power infrastructure for data centers is becoming a real constraint. So even if the demand is there, the question is whether the supply chain can scale fast enough, and the valuations of these companies partly reflect the expectation that they'll capture a large share of the value from that scaling because they're the ones who can actually deliver it.

So I'd read the valuations as the market saying two things at once: compute spending is going to keep growing substantially, and a small number of firms sit on chokepoints in that supply chain. Whether the market is right about the first part is, in some ways, the central question for how fast AI progresses from here.

r001.rationale: The response argues there is room to spend more by comparing compute costs with tech-company revenues and historical programs, but it does not identify larger-scale conventional capital investment as evidence.

r002.rationale: It says chip valuations reflect expectations that AI compute demand and hardware spending will keep growing substantially.

astra-6.text:
I think those valuations suggest that investors expect spending on computing hardware to grow quite substantially. They’re pricing in future profits, so the market seems to be betting that demand for chips—and for the equipment needed to make those chips—will be much larger than it is today.

But I’d be careful about translating those valuations directly into a forecast of how much more compute we’ll buy. A company can become more valuable because investors expect it to capture a larger share of spending or sustain higher margins, rather than because the overall market expands by the same amount. And those expectations could turn out to be wrong.

So I’d take this as evidence that substantial further investment is plausible, rather than as a precise measure of the remaining room to grow. Ultimately, the key question is whether the economic value generated by that compute justifies the spending.

r001.rationale: The response says further investment is plausible, but does not identify the much larger scale of conventional capital investment as evidence for room to expand hardware spending.

r002.rationale: It directly says the valuations suggest investors expect spending on computing hardware to grow substantially.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those valuations are consistent with investors expecting a very substantial increase in spending on compute. If AI becomes a much larger part of the economy, then spending on the hardware that supports it could also become much larger than it is today. And firms like Nvidia, TSMC, and ASML occupy positions where they could capture some of that spending.

But I’d be careful about reading valuations as a direct forecast of how much hardware will be purchased. They also reflect expectations about profit margins, how durable these firms’ competitive advantages are, and how much competition they’ll face. You could have enormous growth in compute spending without all of that translating into profits for today’s leading companies.

So I’d take the valuations as evidence that markets assign meaningful probability to a very large expansion, rather than as a precise estimate of how much more we can spend on computing hardware.

r001.rationale: The response says compute-hardware spending could grow substantially, but does not compare it with the larger scale of conventional capital investment as evidence of room to expand.

r002.rationale: It says the valuations are consistent with investors expecting a very substantial increase in compute spending, including spending on supporting hardware.
